items.title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems
items.text:
Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.

To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, available on Google Cloud.

We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish.

Customers and partners using Gemini 4 Argon

Four ways Argon changes how your business works

1. Hand off your hardest work

Your teams already use Gemini for business to answer questions and draft content. With Argon, they can hand off the deep, multi-step work that used to take hours or days, and get back finished work they can use.

Argon reads long documents that mix text, tables, charts and images, and turns them into one clear output grounded in those sources. It can pull findings from many sources into a single structured answer, analyze data over time, and write stronger legal, finance, and executive documents. On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done. We trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps, and it tells you when it couldn't find something or finish a task.

Customers who tested Argon tell us it excels at turning huge, unstructured inputs into cohesive outputs.

"As software development becomes more agentic, teams need models that can support long-running, multi-step work across all stages of the development lifecycle. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to help organizations bring AI into development, security, and operations while keeping it within established enterprise workflows and controls.” – Stuart Moncada, VP, GitLab.

2. Precise, verifiable results on the work that drives your business

In finance, legal, tax, and other regulated work, calculations and data extraction need to be precise, repeatable, and verifiable.

For financial quantitative work, Argon can help automate multi-step ledger reconciliations, spreadsheet formulas, and variance analyses. It delivers high calculation integrity, citation fidelity, and formula accuracy across quantitative models. The proof is in the numbers: Argon leads on the Vals Index, which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

In legal research, Argon can help legal teams review case law and regulatory filings to pull out verified citations and key precedents. It leads on domain-specific evaluations like Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for legal research and drafting, with strong citation fidelity and direct answers when helping teams evaluate complex legal precedents.

"Gemini 4 Argon shows how much progress Google has made on agentic legal reasoning. We saw substantial improvements over Gemini 3.1 Pro across our legal agent evaluations, particularly in corporate M&A, data privacy and cybersecurity, and EC/VC. Accuracy also held up on long-document analysis, an encouraging result for lawyers working through detailed transactional matters." – Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research, Harvey.

“We collaborated with Google on NowAI-Bench to help shape Gemini 4 for key enterprise work. In early access, it delivered roughly 20% improved task success than Gemini 3.8 Flash, with standout gains in HR and customer service. On the ServiceNow AI Platform, our L1 Service Desk AI specialist brings Google’s most advanced intelligence, governed and secure, turning tasks into fully autonomous work.” - Nenshad Bardoliwalla, Senior Vice President, AI Products, ServiceNow.

3. Build and ship products faster

Argon is built to handle complex, multi-step projects from start to finish. Our customers consistently ask for intelligence that can break down goals, track progress, and update multiple files at the same time.

"Gemini 4 Argon handles complex tasks reliably, from 3D games to rich animations. In Figma Make, it helps teams turn their most ambitious, multi-step ideas into impressive prototypes.” – Loredana Crisan, Chief Design Officer, Figma.

To see how well Argon handles this, we put it to work on our own tools. The team behind our open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) set out to reduce framework overhead and improve code performance while maintaining full compatibility with existing applications. Working autonomously overnight within automated testing guardrails, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and speed up cold imports by 21%. To learn more, read the engineering deep dive here.

Across Google, engineering teams using Argon in Google Antigravity have increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% while cutting code rollbacks by nearly a third. The Chrome team used Argon to finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files in Chromium's 40 million-line codebase, completing months of work in weeks. Argon's improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision and visual coding also make it faster to go from idea to working prototype.

For more advanced algorithms, our code optimization and discovery agent AlphaEvolve uses Argon to deliver strong performance improvements across real-world enterprise workloads, including factory scheduling, logistics, game code speed-ups, and chip layout — as well as complex mathematical benchmarks and more.

To learn how to best use Argon, check out the developer's guide.

4. Stronger defense for your code and business

While Argon has cyber mitigations that block offensive tasks such as pentesting and exploitation, you can still take full advantage of Argon’s defensive capabilities using CodeMender to find and fix vulnerabilities, or use Argon with your own security harness. It ties for first place on CWE-Bench v1 with a top score of 68% for remediating security vulnerabilities.

"We are integrating Gemini 4 Argon into MarketingX for automated codebase security audits. In our evaluations, the model successfully identified 100% of top-priority vulnerabilities with 0% fabricated vulnerabilities across verified claims. This precision unlocks proactive, code-level security for our customers before deployment.” - Yunus Emre, Chief AI Officer of AI Lab, HubX.

Security also means being able to trust Argon inside your own environment. Argon is our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior. It leads the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%. That matters when Argon reads email, documents and webpages that may contain hidden malicious instructions.

We are also releasing Argon without cyber guardrails to a select set of trusted defenders, which allows for testing a full breadth of cybersecurity capabilities. Trusted defenders are vetted through our Fairwind Program, a limited access initiative that provides government, critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity partners exclusive, unmitigated access to advanced models.

Enterprise customers and partners in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.

Business leaders discuss how they are testing and building with Gemini 4 Argon.

Leaders from Amplitude, Deloitte, and Rakuten share Gemini 4 Argon results

Get started

Starting today, Gemini 4 Argon is available in Gemini for business on the web, desktop, and mobile. Enterprise developers and builders can access Argon via API in Gemini platform under model ID gemini-4-argon, in Google AI Studio, and in Google Antigravity.

Argon launches at an introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off. After November 30, standard pricing of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens will apply. Review the model card and developer guide for complete technical specifications, token limits, and migration instructions.

Cyber defenders can join us at Security Summit to learn how to use Gemini 4 Argon to defend against machine-speed threats and automate remediation.

items.title: Cross-cloud conversational analytics made simple with open standards
items.text:
The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting.

Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards.

BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue.

In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language.

Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration.

The borderless lakehouse architecture

This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms.

When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access:

Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define.

Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform.

All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service for Apache Spark. Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution.

Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform.

You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below.

Configure Databricks Unity Catalog

We begin in Databricks by preparing the catalog and table. In Unity Catalog, federated access requires that your target schema be associated with an external location registered in Databricks:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Databricks SQL workspace\r\nCREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db;\r\n\r\n-- Declare the managed target location at the schema level\r\nCREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core \r\n MANAGED LOCATION 's3://my-databricks-bucket/retail/data/';\r\n\r\n-- Create the Iceberg dimension table\r\nCREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products (\r\n product_key INT,\r\n product_id STRING,\r\n product_name STRING,\r\n category STRING,\r\n subcategory STRING,\r\n brand STRING,\r\n price DOUBLE,\r\n cost DOUBLE\r\n)\r\nUSING iceberg;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e08ed90>)])]>

You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided in each section.

Before external engines can read this table, a Databricks metastore administrator must enable External data access on the metastore details tab.

Go to Databricks Admin account and under User Management, create a Databricks Service Principal and make a note of its UUID "6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"

Connect Databricks to BigQuery

Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Databricks workspace URL and the application ID of your Databricks service principal:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"\r\nexport GCP_REGION="us-central1"\r\n\r\ngcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create dbx_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \\\r\n --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \\\r\n --catalog-type="federated" \\\r\n --federated-catalog-type="unity" \\\r\n --unity-instance-name="dbc-xxxxxxxx-xxxx.cloud.databricks.com" \\\r\n --unity-catalog-name="dbx_retail_db" \\\r\n --unity-service-principal-application-id="6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" \\\r\n --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93de49550>)])]>

Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned service account:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe dbx_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93da86c50>)])]>

Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Grant catalog traversal permission\r\nGRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG dbx_retail_db \r\n TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;\r\n\r\n-- Grant schema and read permissions\r\nGRANT USE SCHEMA,EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA dbx_retail_db.dbx_core \r\n TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93d930e90>)])]>

You must grant the EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA privilege to the Databricks Service Principal on the target schemas or catalog to enable credential vending for external data access.

Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details -

Issuer URL* - https://accounts.google.com

Subject* - numeric subject ID returned by the catalog describe command eg 1124251400450xxxxxxxx

Audiences - https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com

Run one query across three clouds

Federated Iceberg tables are addressed in BigQuery using four-part paths: project.catalog.namespace.table.

In our environment, sales transactions reside natively in BigQuery:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS local_retail_dataset\r\nOPTIONS(location="us-central1");\r\n\r\nCREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` (\r\n sale_id STRING,\r\n sale_date DATE,\r\n customer_key INT64,\r\n product_key INT64,\r\n store_key INT64,\r\n quantity INT64,\r\n unit_price NUMERIC,\r\n discount NUMERIC,\r\n total_revenue NUMERIC,\r\n total_cost NUMERIC,\r\n margin NUMERIC\r\n)\r\nPARTITION BY sale_date\r\nCLUSTER BY store_key, product_key;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93d93c8d0>)])]>

We can now run a single SQL query joining our native sales transactions with customer records in Snowflake, product lines in Databricks, and store locations in AWS Glue:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT \r\n c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name, -- From Snowflake Iceberg\r\n p.product_name, -- From Databricks Iceberg\r\n s.store_name, -- From AWS S3 Iceberg\r\n SUM(f.quantity) AS total_units_sold, -- From BigQuery native fact\r\n SUM(f.total_revenue) AS total_sales_revenue -- From BigQuery native fact\r\nFROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f\r\nINNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c \r\n ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key\r\nINNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p \r\n ON f.product_key = p.product_key\r\nINNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s \r\n ON f.store_key = s.store_key\r\nGROUP BY 1, 2, 3\r\nORDER BY total_sales_revenue DESC\r\nLIMIT 10;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93fe28f90>)])]>

BigQuery processes the joins in place. Notice that Snowflake identifiers appear in uppercase (CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS), while Databricks and AWS Glue maintain lowercase table paths.

Figure 2 - Query results combining data across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue.

Explore cross-cloud data with natural language

Because federated Iceberg tables behave like native tables within BigQuery, downstream analytical features inherit access directly. You can point conversational analytics in BigQuery at these federated schemas to let team members explore cross-cloud data using natural language prompts.

To give conversational analytics full operational context, we save our federated join as a logical view:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.v_omnichannel_sales_pulse` AS\r\nSELECT \r\n f.sale_id,\r\n f.sale_date,\r\n c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name,\r\n c.country AS customer_country,\r\n p.product_name,\r\n p.category AS product_category,\r\n p.brand AS product_brand,\r\n s.store_name,\r\n s.city AS store_city,\r\n s.region AS store_region,\r\n f.quantity,\r\n f.total_revenue,\r\n f.margin\r\nFROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f\r\nINNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c \r\n ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key\r\nINNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p \r\n ON f.product_key = p.product_key\r\nINNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s \r\n ON f.store_key = s.store_key;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93fe2b290>)])]>

Analyze sales performance in natural language

When you ask conversational analytics in BigQuery:

"Who are our top customers by total sales revenue, what products did they buy, and which stores did they shop at?"

Conversational analytics evaluates the schema across all three remote catalogs, generates the SQL statement, executes the query, and presents the response.

Figure 3: Conversational analytics in BigQuery translates plain-language prompts into federated queries across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue.

Plan for caching and data residency

Before deploying federated catalogs in production, consider these operational behaviors:

Background refresh timing: The --refresh-interval flag controls metadata synchronization. The minimum interval is 300 seconds. For larger catalogs containing hundreds of tables, metadata retrieval can take longer. If a sync cycle overruns, BigQuery skips the next scheduled run to avoid task queuing.

Automatic query caching: BigQuery caches retrieved cross-cloud data blocks in the region where your federated catalog resides (e.g. us-central1). This helps reduce network transfer on repeated queries. Because cached blocks reside within Google Cloud storage in that region, confirm that this aligns with your organization's data residency policies.

Encryption controls: Cross-cloud cache blocks use Google-managed encryption keys. If your organization enforces the constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices policy constraint, BigQuery bypasses the cache and reads directly from remote storage for every query.

Monitoring access metrics: You can evaluate cache utilization in your query execution plans. Check the objectStorageStats section in BigQuery job statistics to compare cacheBytesRead against objectStorageBytesRead.

Next steps

In summary, Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse helps you activate your data regardless of where it lives without costly migrations or building additional data pipelines. Get started today by reviewing the borderless Lakehouse architecture documentation to learn more about supported regions and credential configurations. You can work through the borderless Lakehouse codelab to practice federating external catalogs step-by-step. Finally, connect with your Google Cloud account team or customer engineer to evaluate borderless lakehouse patterns for your specific data platforms or industries.

Appendix

Setting up Snowflake and AWS Glue cross cloud data access

Connect Snowflake and Big Query

Configure Snowflake Horizon Catalog

We begin in Snowflake by creating the database, schema, and Iceberg table. In Snowflake Horizon, managed Iceberg tables expose an open Apache Iceberg REST catalog interface automatically:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet\r\nCREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db;\r\nCREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db.core;\r\n\r\n-- Create the Iceberg dimension table\r\nCREATE OR REPLACE ICEBERG TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers (\r\n customer_key INTEGER,\r\n customer_id VARCHAR,\r\n first_name VARCHAR,\r\n last_name VARCHAR,\r\n email VARCHAR,\r\n gender VARCHAR,\r\n country VARCHAR,\r\n signup_date DATE\r\n\r\n)\r\nCATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE'\r\nEXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93fe28390>)])]>

Before external engines can read this catalog, configure a dedicated reader role and grant traversal permissions across the database, schema, and table.

SQL

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Create a dedicated reader role\r\nCREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;\r\n\r\n-- Grant database and schema traversal permissions\r\nGRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sf_retail_db TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;\r\nGRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sf_retail_db.core TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;\r\n\r\n-- Grant read access on the target table\r\nGRANT SELECT ON TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd960177fd0>)])]>

Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Snowflake account identifier, the reader role, and the root Iceberg database name:

bash

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"\r\nexport GCP_REGION="us-central1"\r\n\r\ngcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create sf_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \\\r\n --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \\\r\n --catalog-type="federated" \\\r\n --federated-catalog-type="snowflake" \\\r\n --snowflake-account-identifier="xy12345-ab67890" \\\r\n --snowflake-warehouse="SF_RETAIL_DB" \\\r\n --snowflake-role="gcp_lakehouse_reader_role" \\\r\n --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93fe296d0>)])]>

In the Apache Iceberg REST specification, --snowflake-warehouse references the catalog root database name (SF_RETAIL_DB), not a virtual compute warehouse.

Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned numeric service account ID:

bash

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe sf_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \\\r\n --format=\'value(biglake-service-account-id)\''), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93ff99e10>)])]>

Return to Snowflake to bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user via Workload Identity Federation (WIF):

SQL

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet\r\nUSE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;\r\n\r\n-- Bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user\r\nCREATE OR REPLACE USER snowflake_service_user\r\n TYPE = SERVICE\r\n WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = (\r\n TYPE = GCP\r\n SUBJECT = '102669xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx' -- Numeric subject ID returned by gcloud describe\r\n )\r\n DEFAULT_ROLE = gcp_lakehouse_reader_role\r\n COMMENT = 'Service user for Lakehouse catalog federation over WIF';\r\n\r\n-- Grant the reader role to this service user\r\nGRANT ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role TO USER snowflake_service_user;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93ff9bc10>)])]>

This establishes passwordless authentication over OpenID Connect, allowing BigQuery to discover table metadata and vend temporary query-time credentials directly from Snowflake Horizon.

Configure AWS Glue Data Catalog

We begin in AWS by preparing the IAM identity, establishing access permissions across AWS Glue and Amazon S3, and registering the Iceberg table.

First, create a placeholder trust policy named trust_policy.json. This allows you to provision the AWS IAM role before Google Cloud assigns the unique catalog service agent:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '{\r\n "Version": "2012-10-17",\r\n "Statement": [\r\n {\r\n "Effect": "Allow",\r\n "Principal": {\r\n "Federated": "accounts.google.com"\r\n },\r\n "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",\r\n "Condition": {\r\n "StringEquals": {\r\n "accounts.google.com:aud": ["PLACEHOLDER_VALUE"],\r\n "accounts.google.com:sub": ["PLACEHOLDER_VALUE"]\r\n }\r\n }\r\n }\r\n ]\r\n}'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93ff9bb90>)])]>

Create the IAM role using the AWS CLI. Setting a 12-hour session duration (43200 seconds) prevents credential expiration during long-running analytical queries:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export AWS_ROLE_NAME="lakehouse_glue_federation_role"\r\n\r\naws iam create-role \\\r\n --role-name "$AWS_ROLE_NAME" \\\r\n --assume-role-policy-document file://trust_policy.json \\\r\n --max-session-duration 43200'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93da11450>)])]>

Next, define the permissions policy in a file named permissions_policy.json. This policy grants BigQuery permission to read the AWS Glue catalog metadata and access the underlying Parquet data files in Amazon S3:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '{\r\n "Version": "2012-10-17",\r\n "Statement": [\r\n {\r\n "Sid": "GlueCatalogRead",\r\n "Effect": "Allow",\r\n "Action": [\r\n "glue:GetCatalog",\r\n "glue:GetDatabase",\r\n "glue:GetDatabases",\r\n "glue:GetTable",\r\n "glue:GetTables"\r\n ],\r\n "Resource": "arn:aws:glue:us-east-2:123456789012:*"\r\n },\r\n {\r\n "Sid": "S3BucketAndObjectRead",\r\n "Effect": "Allow",\r\n "Action": [\r\n "s3:ListBucket",\r\n "s3:GetObject"\r\n ],\r\n "Resource": [\r\n "arn:aws:s3:::my-glue-iceberg-bucket",\r\n "arn:aws:s3:::my-glue-iceberg-bucket/*"\r\n ]\r\n }\r\n ]\r\n}'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e15e410>)])]>

Attach this permissions policy to your newly created role:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'aws iam put-role-policy \\\r\n --role-name "$AWS_ROLE_NAME" \\\r\n --policy-name "lakehouse_glue_federation_policy" \\\r\n --policy-document file://permissions_policy.json'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e15db90>)])]>

Important (AWS Lake Formation): If your AWS environment uses AWS Lake Formation, verify that the IAMAllowedPrincipals group has access to the target database and table (or grant explicit Lake Formation permissions to lakehouse_glue_federation_role if the bucket is registered with AWS Lake Formation). Without this, Lake Formation security settings will block the IAM role from accessing catalog metadata.

With permissions in place, create the database and Iceberg table in AWS Glue using Amazon Athena:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Amazon Athena\r\nCREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS glue_retail_db;\r\n\r\nCREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS glue_retail_db.dim_stores (\r\n store_key INT,\r\n store_id STRING,\r\n store_name STRING,\r\n city STRING,\r\n state STRING,\r\n region STRING,\r\n manager STRING,\r\n opened_date DATE\r\n\r\n)\r\nLOCATION 's3://my-glue-iceberg-bucket/retail/dim_stores/'\r\nTBLPROPERTIES (\r\n 'table_type'='ICEBERG', \r\n 'format'='parquet', \r\n 'write_compression'='zstd' \r\n\r\n);"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9600b2150>)])]>

Connect AWS Glue to BigQuery

Next, register the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your 12-digit AWS Account ID, AWS Region, and the role ARN created above:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"\r\nexport GCP_REGION="us-central1"\r\nexport AWS_REGION="us-east-2"\r\nexport AWS_ACCOUNT_ID="123456789012"\r\n\r\ngcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create glue_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \\\r\n --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \\\r\n --catalog-type="federated" \\\r\n --federated-catalog-type="glue" \\\r\n --glue-warehouse="$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID" \\\r\n --glue-aws-region="$AWS_REGION" \\\r\n --glue-aws-role-arn="arn:aws:iam::${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:role/lakehouse_glue_federation_role"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9600b22d0>)])]>

To prevent premature background refresh failures while the AWS trust policy propagates, initialize the catalog without setting a refresh schedule.

Next, extract the unique numeric subject ID assigned to the catalog by Google Cloud:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export LAKEHOUSE_SA_ID=$(gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe glue_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \\\r\n --format="value(biglake-service-account-id)")\r\n\r\necho "Assigned Lakehouse Service Account ID: $LAKEHOUSE_SA_ID"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9600b1050>)])]>

Return to the AWS CLI and update your IAM role's trust policy, replacing the placeholder with the verified Google Cloud identity:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat > trust_policy_final.json << EOF\r\n{\r\n "Version": "2012-10-17",\r\n "Statement": [\r\n {\r\n "Effect": "Allow",\r\n "Principal": {\r\n "Federated": "accounts.google.com"\r\n },\r\n "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",\r\n "Condition": {\r\n "StringEquals": {\r\n "accounts.google.com:aud": [\r\n "$LAKEHOUSE_SA_ID"\r\n ],\r\n "accounts.google.com:sub": [\r\n "$LAKEHOUSE_SA_ID"\r\n ]\r\n }\r\n }\r\n }\r\n ]\r\n}\r\nEOF\r\n\r\naws iam update-assume-role-policy \\\r\n --role-name "$AWS_ROLE_NAME" \\\r\n --policy-document file://trust_policy_final.json'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93fffcf90>)])]>

5. Enable metadata synchronization and verify

bash

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs update glue_retail_db \\\r\n --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \\\r\n --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93ffff890>)])]>

Verify that the namespaces are discovered and synchronized:

bash

code_block

items.title: Bringing our latest frontier model to Android Developers
items.text:
Posted by Jason Buchel, Creative Technologist, Platform & Devices

As agentic development accelerates, Android engineering is reaching an exciting new frontier: moving from assistive code completion to agents executing end-to-end under your direction. You have total choice and flexibility in the models and agents you use.

Gemini 4 Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science.

Starting today, Android developers can access Gemini 4 Argon across their development surfaces, including Google Antigravity (standalone and in Android Studio Canary) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and in Android Studio and Google AI Studio via the paid tier of the Gemini API.

Velocity & Autonomy: Closed-loop build self-correction

Argon has significant improvements in long-horizon autonomous execution and the ability to plan and run multi-step, complex software tasks over time.

Self-Healing Build Loops: When a local build fails, the Antigravity execution harness captures error streams directly from Gradle daemons and Kotlin compiler logs. Using this feedback, the model iteratively diagnoses the root-cause of build failures to arrive at a revised solution. Gemini 4 Argon's training dramatically improves on this process. It's engineered to maintain a consistent hypothesis across successive rounds of editing, as well as making use of internal Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) awareness to better inform edits. This means Gemini 4 Argon is more resilient and better able to address the true root-cause of build failures.

UI sophistication: Fluid motion & shader-backed Jetpack Compose

Argon demonstrates exceptional design craft, generating production-ready Jetpack Compose code out of the box:

AGSL Shaders on the GPU: Argon possesses the advanced mathematical reasoning needed to write complex, production-ready Android Graphics Shading Language (AGSL) directly into Compose Modifier.graphicsLayer blocks and shader brushes. From live frosted glass shaders to dynamic lighting and ripple effects, Argon can handle complicated vector and rendering math that produces lightweight GPU shaders that run alongside fluid 120 FPS Compose animations.

A flexible developer experience with Android CLI

Antigravity operates across multiple surfaces, from the desktop app and IDE extensions to the command line. No matter which surface you prefer, the official Android CLI plugin is the de-facto engine that connects your agent to local Android tools, enabling it to run programmatic commands for common tasks and execute custom developer skills.

Starting today, you can access and configure this agentic workspace in two primary ways:

Setting up visually (Antigravity Desktop & Android Studio Canary)

In the Antigravity Desktop App: Go to Settings > Customizations > Build With Google Plugins (or the Antigravity Plugin Marketplace), locate android-cli-plugin, and toggle it to Enabled

In Android Studio Canary: Log in to your Antigravity account in the agent tool window to enable agentic workflows directly alongside your editor

Setting up via the Terminal CLI

For Google Antigravity, run:

agy plugin install android-cli-plugin

For any terminal agent (via Android CLI), run:

android init

Availability & getting started

Starting today, Argon is rolling out globally to developers in supported regions. You can access and begin building with the model in your local environment across three primary development surfaces:

Google Antigravity: Google AI Ultra subscribers can build with Gemini 4 Argon in the standalone Antigravity desktop app (available for macOS, Windows, and Linux) or directly via the terminal CLI

Android Studio:

Via Google Antigravity: Google AI Ultra subscribers can build with Gemini 4 Argon by logging into Antigravity within the latest Android Studio Canary.

Via the Gemini API: Developers on the paid tier of the Gemini API can build with Gemini 4 Argon in Android Studio.

Google AI Studio: Google AI Ultra subscribers or developers on the paid tier of the Gemini API can build with Gemini 4 Argon via Playground and Build in Google AI Studio.

Firebase AI Logic: Starting today, developers globally on the paid tier of the Gemini API can use Gemini 4 Argon client-side to build intelligent features in their mobile and web apps via Firebase AI Logic.

To begin building with Argon in your local environment:

Choose your path: Confirm you have an active Google AI Ultra subscription to use Antigravity, or ensure you are on the paid tier of the Gemini API to use standard API surfaces (with introductory pricing available through November 30, 2026).

Update your tools: Download the latest version of the Antigravity desktop app or CLI, and install the official Android CLI plugin (agy plugin install android-cli-plugin) to connect your agentic workspace directly to your Android Studio build tools.

We are eager to see the high-craft Android experiences you build at the frontier. Share your projects and feedback with us on X (@AndroidDev) and LinkedIn!

items.title: One Agent Development Kit, five languages
items.text:
When we talk about agents, that doesn't necessarily mean we're talking about Python. In today's modern ecosystem, an agent might run as a high-concurrency Go microservice on Cloud Run, or live inside a browser tab calling Chrome's on-device model. Yet many agent frameworks assume a Python-only stack. That assumption forces teams to either spin up a Python service just for their agent workloads, or to build agent orchestration logic from scratch in their own language.

Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) removes that trade-off with coverage for Python, Go, TypeScript, Java, and Kotlin. Each version of the ADK is built from the ground up for its own runtime and type system, while sharing a unified architecture with interoperability through open protocols.

A shared foundation

Picking a language doesn't lock in your architecture: all five support the same open protocols. ADK includes a Model Context Protocol client in every language, so a custom tool exposed as an MCP server can be called from any of them immediately.

For multi-agent systems, ADK supports the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, allowing an agent to communicate with a remote agent over HTTP. Through A2A, agents written in different languages or frameworks are interoperable.

Starting agent-first

To get started, run the one-time setup command to check your Google Cloud authentication, install the CLI, and then set up first-party ADK skills in coding agents like Antigravity, Claude Code, or Codex:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'uvx google-agents-cli setup'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e2b2290>)])]>

Then, run the scaffold command to generate a working project with A2A endpoints and deployment config for Cloud Run, Gemini Enterprise Agent Runtime, or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE):

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Scaffold an ADK project (use --agent adk for Python or --agent adk_go for Go)\r\nagents-cli scaffold create my-go-agent \\\r\n --agent adk_go \\\r\n --deployment-target cloud_run \\\r\n --region us-central1'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e2b0d90>)])]>

Both the ADK for Python and ADK for Kotlin repositories also ship agent builder skills in their source trees, and the adk.dev/llms.txt resource gives any coding agent on-demand API documentation across all five languages.

Coding-agent skills scaffold your project while MCP and A2A connect all five language runtimes.

Hands-on view of each ADK

The clearest way to feel the difference between the five languages is to define the same weather tool in each one and see how its design fits the runtime.

Python

In ADK for Python, you don't need a decorator or a schema builder class. You pass a plain Python function into the tools parameter, and ADK inspects its signature, type hints, and docstring at startup to automatically construct the tool declaration and Pydantic parameter schema:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent\r\n\r\n\r\ndef get_weather(city: str) -> dict:\r\n """Retrieves the current weather report for a specified city.\r\n\r\n Args:\r\n city (str): The name of the city for which to retrieve the weather report.\r\n """\r\n return {"status": "success", "report": f"Sunny and 72F in {city}."}\r\n\r\n\r\nroot_agent = Agent(\r\n name="weather_agent",\r\n model="gemini-3.8-flash",\r\n instruction="Answer questions about the weather in a city.",\r\n tools=[get_weather],\r\n)'), ('language', 'lang-py'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e2b1690>)])]>

Beyond fast prototyping, Python is ADK's reference implementation, shipping the broadest set of Google Cloud integrations (BigQuery, Spanner, Bigtable) and model adapters (Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI, LiteLLM). Paired with the adk eval or agents-cli eval run commands, its evaluation tooling scores agent trajectories against golden datasets in continuous integration (CI) to test the whole system end to end, even when your production service runs in another language.

Go

While Python leads in experimentation and evaluation, ADK for Go hits the sweet spot for production backend engineering.

A Go tool function takes the agent.Context configuration and a strongly typed input struct. The functiontool.New function uses Go generics to infer both the input and output schemas from your struct tags:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'type GetWeatherArgs struct {\r\n\tCity string `json:"city" jsonschema:"The city to look up weather for."`\r\n}\r\n\r\ntype GetWeatherResult struct {\r\n\tReport string `json:"report"`\r\n}\r\n\r\nfunc getWeather(_ agent.Context, args GetWeatherArgs) (GetWeatherResult, error) {\r\n\treturn GetWeatherResult{Report: "Sunny and 72F in " + args.City}, nil\r\n}\r\n\r\nweatherTool, err := functiontool.New(functiontool.Config{\r\n\tName: "get_weather",\r\n\tDescription: "Retrieves the current weather report for a city.",\r\n}, getWeather)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd93e2b3b10>)])]>

Because the functiontool.New function is generic over your handler's signature, the Go compiler verifies that your function matches the expected contract before your binary ever runs.

Go was also the first language after Python to ship the ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow runtime. When you need deterministic control flow alongside LLM reasoning, the workflow.New function wires agents and plain Go functions into a directed graph with conditional routing and parallel steps:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'ag, err := workflowagent.New("order_pipeline", []workflow.Edge{\r\n\t{From: workflow.Start, To: triageNode},\r\n\t{From: triageNode, To: fulfillNode, Route: workflow.StringRoute("fulfill")},\r\n\t{From: fulfillNode, To: notifyNode},\r\n})'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9604acc90>)])]>

Where Go really stands out is in production on Cloud Run and GKE. A compiled Go agent packages onto a roughly 2 MiB Google distroless static base image, with no language VM or heavy dependency tree. A static Go binary binds to its port as soon as the container starts, skipping the module imports of dynamic languages and the JAR unpacking and JIT warmup of JVM services.

After it's running, Go's concurrency model fits agent workloads naturally. Each goroutine starts with a 2 KB stack and minimal scheduling overhead, so a single instance can multiplex thousands of concurrent streaming requests and tool calls. ADK for Go also includes built-in A2A server handlers and OpenTelemetry tracing out of the box.

TypeScript

TypeScript erases type annotations when compiling to JavaScript, so runtime reflection isn't an option. Instead, ADK for TypeScript pairs with Zod. You pass a z.object(...) schema to the FunctionTool function, and TypeScript statically infers the parameter types of your execute callback from that single declaration:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import { FunctionTool, LlmAgent } from "@google/adk";\r\nimport { z } from "zod";\r\n\r\nconst getWeatherTool = new FunctionTool({\r\n name: "get_weather",\r\n description: "Retrieves the current weather report for a city.",\r\n parameters: z.object({\r\n city: z.string().describe("The name of the city."),\r\n }),\r\n execute: async ({ city }) => {\r\n return { status: "success", report: `Sunny and 72F in ${city}.` };\r\n },\r\n});\r\n\r\nexport const rootAgent = new LlmAgent({\r\n name: "weather_agent",\r\n model: "gemini-3.8-flash",\r\n instruction: "Answer questions about the weather in a city.",\r\n tools: [getWeatherTool],\r\n});'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9604ade10>)])]>

Your runtime input validation, the JSON Schema sent to the model, and your IDE autocomplete inside the execute callback all flow from one source of truth.

TypeScript also runs on the ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow engine and ships a standalone browser bundle. Beyond Node.js services, you can run an ADK agent directly in a browser tab using WebMCP for page-level tools and Chrome's on-device Prompt API.

Java

ADK for Java snaps right in for teams who have standardized on Maven, Gradle, and Spring Boot. You add @Schema annotations to method parameters and assemble agents by using a fluent LlmAgent.builder() API:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'public class WeatherTools {\r\n public static Map<String, String> getWeather(\r\n @Schema(name = "city", description = "The name of the city")\r\n String city) {\r\n return Map.of("status", "success", "report", "Sunny and 72F in " + city);\r\n }\r\n}\r\n\r\nLlmAgent agent = LlmAgent.builder()\r\n .name("weather_agent")\r\n .model("gemini-3.8-flash")\r\n .instruction("Answer questions about the weather in a city.")\r\n .tools(FunctionTool.create(WeatherTools.class, "getWeather"))\r\n .build();'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9604af3d0>)])]>

At runtime, the runner streams agent events reactively through RxJava. For local testing and existing JVM apps, ADK for Java ships a Maven Dev UI plugin alongside first-party bridges for Spring AI and LangChain4j.

Kotlin

ADK for Kotlin takes a strong stance on build-time safety. Its Kotlin Symbol Processing (KSP) compiler plugin reads @Tool and @Param annotations at build time and emits the tool schema directly into bytecode:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'class WeatherTools {\r\n @Tool(\r\n name = "get_weather",\r\n description = "Retrieves the current weather report for a city.",\r\n )\r\n suspend fun getWeather(\r\n @Param("The name of the city.") city: String\r\n ): Map<String, String> = mapOf("status" to "success", "report" to "Sunny and 72F in $city")\r\n}\r\n\r\nval agent = LlmAgent(\r\n model = Gemini("gemini-3.8-flash"),\r\n name = "weather_agent",\r\n instruction = Instruction("Answer questions about the weather in a city."),\r\n tools = WeatherTools().generatedTools(),\r\n)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd9604afb50>)])]>

If a tool signature uses an unsupported type or declares a default value on a non-nullable parameter, your Gradle build fails immediately instead of breaking in production. Because the .generatedTools() function uses zero runtime reflection, it survives Android R8 shrinking.

That zero-reflection design makes it possible to run the entire agent loop locally on Android. It offers JVM server support, including a Spring AI bridge and experimental ADK 2.0 graph workflows. On-device, ADK for Kotlin integrates with LiteRT-LM for tool calling and ML Kit (Gemini Nano) for text generation. It also works with Room and AppSearch for local state, and Android AppFunctions for OS-level actions, all without requiring a network connection.

Choice without compromise

Having five native languages in ADK means you don't have to pick a single runtime for your entire organization. Because every version of ADK speaks MCP and A2A, each component of your system can use the language that fits it best.

What languages have you used to build agents with Google's ADK? Let me know what stack you're running on X, LinkedIn, or Bluesky.

items.title: Cloud Release Notes — October 13, 2026
items.text:
BigQuery

Feature

The AI.AGG function is generally available (GA). You can use this function to semantically aggregate unstructured input data based on natural language instructions.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend

Limitations of spend cap budgets

Configure a spend cap budget

Lift an enforced spend cap

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

Using the Cloud Billing Budget API for spend cap budgets

Spend cap budget concepts and limitations

Create a spend cap budget

Lift an enforced spend cap

Cloud Billing Budget API REST reference

Cloud SDK

Breaking

589.0.0 (2026-10-13)

Breaking Changes

(Google Cloud CLI) Deprecated the skaffold component in Google Cloud CLI. The component will be removed from Google Cloud CLI releases after January 15, 2027. A portion of gcloud components install skaffold attempts now return an error. Please install Skaffold following the instructions at https://skaffold.dev/docs/install/.

Google Cloud CLI

Updated Linux and Windows bundled Python to install cryptography 46.0.7 from the official PyPI wheels instead of custom builds.

Updated the Alpine-based Docker images (:alpine, :VERSION-alpine) to use a bundled Python and no longer include a system python3.

Updated bundled Python to 3.14.8 on Linux and Windows, and in the Alpine-based Docker images. This updates the OpenSSL that Python uses for TLS to 3.5.9.

AlloyDB

Added --enable-express flag to gcloud beta alloydb clusters create|update.

Apigee

Promoted gcloud apigee apis delete to GA. The command deletes an API proxy and all of its revisions. Every command in gcloud apigee apis now serves GA.

Fixed an issue where gcloud apigee apis import --from-template discarded a template's endpoints and targets whenever the template referenced a feature. A template that declared its own topology and used features only for policies compiled to a proxy with no ProxyEndpoint, and the import failed. A template's endpoints and targets now seed the proxy, and features are applied on top of them.

App Engine

Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run dropped the Serverless VPC Access connector for deployed versions.

Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run mapped App Engine Flexible instance_ip_mode to Cloud Run ingress.

Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run did not route all egress through Direct VPC for internal-only App Engine Flexible apps.

App Lifecycle Manager

Hid the deprecated gcloud beta saas-runtime command group. Existing commands continue to work and print a deprecation warning. Use gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager instead.

Beyondcorp

Deprecated gcloud beta beyondcorp app command group.

BigLake

Added --service-directory-name flag to gcloud biglake delta-sharing catalogs update.

BigQuery

Added support for Azure Data Lake Storage URIs (abfs:// and abfss://) in inline external table definitions (--external_table_definition).

Added --dataplex_entry_group flag to bq mk --transfer_config and bq update --transfer_config to allow integration with Dataplex Entry Groups.

Added support to filter Transfer Configs by Dataplex Entry Group using --filter="metadata_destination.dataplex_configuration:*" for bq ls --transfer_config.

Cloud Alerting

Promoted gcloud monitoring alerts command group to GA.

Cloud Composer

Updated gcloud composer environments storage dags export, gcloud composer environments storage data export, gcloud composer environments storage plugins export, gcloud beta composer environments storage dags export, gcloud beta composer environments storage data export, and gcloud beta composer environments storage plugins export to skip, with a warning, objects that would be written outside of the local --destination directory.

Cloud DNS

Added gcloud beta dns outbound-endpoints command group.

Added --outbound-endpoints flag to gcloud beta dns managed-zones and gcloud beta dns policies.

Cloud Firestore

Promoted gcloud firestore change-streams commands to GA.

Cloud Storage

Added server-side hash validation by default for resumable uploads in gcloud storage cp, gcloud storage mv, and gcloud storage rsync. To disable this behavior, run gcloud config set storage/enable_server_side_hash_validation False.

Compute Engine

Optimized gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances by passing --limit and --page-size to the backend API and terminating page fetching early when the limit is reached.

Added CMEK_ENCRYPTION option to --local-ssd-encryption-mode flag of gcloud beta compute instances create to encrypt Local SSDs with customer-managed encryption keys.

Fixed gcloud beta compute disk-types list returning no results when --zones or --regions is specified. Deprecated NAME positional argument and --regexp flag of this command. Use --filter instead.

Promoted loadBalancingScheme value EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH to GA in import and export schemas for gcloud compute backend-services.

Promoted IPAddresses and loadBalancingScheme value EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH to GA in import and export schemas for gcloud compute forwarding-rules.

Promoted gcloud compute advice capacity to GA.

Promoted gcloud compute advice capacity-history to GA.

Database Migration

Updated --ssl-flags flag documentation and parsing for gcloud database-migration connection-profiles commands to support custom delimiter syntax (^DELIM^) for values containing commas (e.g. server_certificate_dn).

Added --dbm-port flag to gcloud database-migration connection-profiles create sqlserver and gcloud database-migration connection-profiles update commands to specify the Database Mirroring (DBM) port for SQL Server Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations.

Added --sqlserver-dag-source-ag and --sqlserver-dag-linked-server flags to gcloud database-migration migration-jobs create and gcloud database-migration migration-jobs update commands to configure SQL Server Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations.

Device Run

Removed gcloud beta device-run sessions submit xctest. The command remains available in the alpha release track.

GKE Hub

Added --prioritized flag to gcloud beta container fleet rolloutsequences upgrade and gcloud beta container hub rolloutsequences upgrade.

Kubernetes Engine

Added --wiz-sensor-api-key-secret-uri, --wiz-sensor-proxy-secret-uri, and --wiz-sensor-registry-secret-uri flags to gcloud container clusters create, create-auto, and update commands to configure Wiz Sensor.

Looker

Fixed gcloud looker instances update --linked-lsp-project-number sending an empty update mask and failing.

Oracle Database

Added update command to the following gcloud oracle-database command groups to support adding, updating, removing, and clearing labels using --update-labels, --remove-labels, and --clear-labels flags:

gcloud oracle-database cloud-exadata-infrastructures update

gcloud oracle-database cloud-vm-clusters update

gcloud oracle-database db-systems update

gcloud oracle-database exascale-db-storage-vaults update

gcloud oracle-database goldengate-connections update

gcloud oracle-database goldengate-connection-assignments update

gcloud oracle-database goldengate-deployments update

gcloud oracle-database odb-networks odb-subnets update

Workbench

Fixed --nic-type flag choices in gcloud workbench instances create to use VIRTIO_NET instead of VIRTIGO_NET.

Subscribe to these release notes at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/google-cloud-sdk-announce.

Dataform

Feature

You can use Developer Connect to connect Dataform repositories to Secure Source Manager repositories. This feature is in Preview.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon is available in AlphaEvolve

AlphaEvolve experiments can generate candidate programs with Gemini 4 Argon in the global, us, and eu regions. To use it, specify gemini-4-argon in the models field of generationSettings. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Supported models and AlphaEvolve limitations.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It supports a 1,048,576-token context window (shared across input, thinking, and output tokens), configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation tokens on the GenerateContent API, and agentic video understanding in GA.

Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive (gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive), a version of Gemini 4 Argon for defensive cybersecurity use cases, is also available in GA behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

Known issue (long decodes): Long decoding (continuation_token) on the GenerateContent API (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path.

For more information, see Get started with Gemini 4 and the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon.

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Argon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-argon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Managed Service for Apache Airflow

Feature

Development mode environments and Environment hibernation are now generally available (GA).

You can now create Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environments with Airflow 3 in development mode to test and develop DAGs before publishing them to production. You can hibernate development mode environments when you no longer need them. Hibernation reduces most environment costs to zero.

items.title: Find your routine next steps on the post-meeting screen in Google Meet
items.text:
We are introducing next steps in Google Meet. Powered by Gemini and Workspace Studio, our new capability allows users to automate repetitive post-meeting tasks directly within Google Workspace. Next steps help you transform meeting discussions into definitive actions, like drafting follow-up emails in Gmail or exporting action items to Google Tasks.

During busy work days, meetings are frequently just one part of an expanding workflow. Without the right integrations, capturing decisions and executing on follow-up tasks requires manual data entry that leads to context fragmentation and wasted time.

On your post-meeting screen, look for the section titled, “Routines for this meeting,” where you can enable next steps with one tap. “Take notes for me” must be enabled during the meeting for any next steps to appear. This works for both one-off or recurring meetings, and users can enable a specific next step across all of their meetings (when “Take notes for me” is turned on).

We are starting out with just two routine next steps, draft a follow-up email and add action items to Google Tasks. However, there are several more soon on the way, so be on the lookout!

Draft a followup email or export your action items to Google Tasks on the Google Meet post-call page after a one-off meeting

You can also complete your next steps after a recurring meeting

Getting started

Admins: This feature will be ON by default and can be disabled at the domain/OU/group level via the Workspace Studio Admin settings or the Take Notes for Me setting. Visit the Help Center to learn more.

End users: This feature is available to users when "Take notes for me" is enabled. Users can manage their routine next steps from the Meet post-call screen or in the Workspace Studio Flows library once turned on for the first time in Google Meet. Visit the Help Center to learn more.

Rollout pace

Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains: Extended rollout (potentially longer than 15 days for feature visibility) started on October 5, 2026

Availability

Business: Business Standard and Plus

Enterprise: Enterprise Standard and Plus

Education Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education

Resources

Google Help: Complete routine tasks with post-meeting next steps

items.title: Configure Access Management and Access Approvals policies using classification labels with rules in Assured Controls
items.text:
We’re introducing Assured Controls rules in the Google Workspace Admin Console, giving administrators a more granular, resource-centric way to enforce Access Management and Access Approvals policies on Google Drive files.

Previously, Access Management and Access Approvals policies could only be scoped at the user level, applying broadly to all covered data owned by users within a selected Organizational Unit (OU) or group. With Assured Controls rules, admins can now configure both Access Management and Access Approvals policies together in a single unified rule and target specific Google Drive files using classification labels in addition to existing OU and group-based scoping capabilities.

By scoping Assured Controls policies to specific classification labels, organizations can reserve their strictest sovereign and compliance controls for only their most sensitive files while maintaining standard, rapid support workflows for less sensitive business data.

How organizations can use Assured Controls rules:

Automated end-to-end protection with Data Loss Prevention (DLP): Admins can combine data protection rules with Assured Controls rules to automatically apply Access Approvals and Access Management policies based on Drive file contents. A DLP rule can automatically apply a classification label when sensitive content (such as Personally Identifiable Information, financial records, or regulated project identifiers) is detected in a Drive file, which then automatically triggers the corresponding Assured Controls rule using that label as a condition to enforce Access Management and Access Approvals protections.

Regional data sovereignty across multinational teams: Multinational enterprises can apply regional classification labels (such as EU Restricted or U.S. Restricted) to Drive files and restrict access to EU or US support staff based on the contents of the file itself.

Targeted compliance for regulated workloads: Public sector and financial services organizations can apply a classification label (such as CJIS / IRS 1075) to sensitive Drive files and use an Assured Controls rule to restrict support actions on those files to CJIS-authorized and IRS 1075-authorized individuals while simultaneously requiring explicit Access Approvals—without impacting support speed for unclassified files owned by the same users.

Getting started

Admins: Use our Help Center to learn more about Assured Controls rules for Access Management & Access Approvals.

End users: There is no end user setting for this feature.

Rollout pace

Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains: Gradual rollout (up to 15 days for feature visibility) started on September 30, 2026

Availability

Access Approvals rule-based enforcement: Available to Google Workspace Enterprise Plus and Frontline Plus customers with the Assured Controls or Assured Controls Plus add-on.

Access Management rule-based enforcement: Available to Google Workspace Enterprise Plus and Frontline Plus customers with the Assured Controls Plus add on.

Resources

Google Workspace Admin Help: Assured Controls rules for Access Management & Access Approvals

Google Workspace Admin Help: Access Management: Limit the Google staff who can take support actions related to your data

Google Workspace Admin Help: Access Approvals: Require Google staff to request approval before viewing support data

Google Workspace Admin Help: About Assured Controls and Assured Controls Plus

Google Workspace Admin Help: What data is covered by Access Management and Access Approvals?

Google Workspace Admin Help: Create data protection rules

Google Workspace Admin Help: Create classification labels for your organization

items.title: Introducing the Googlebook Linux Terminal Preview: A VM-Backed Environment for AI and Development
items.text:
Posted by Cyrus Stoller, Group Product Manager, Laptops & Tablets

Today, getting the most out of AI workflows requires access to a terminal with a command line, even if someone doesn’t identify as a programmer or software developer. With Googlebook, we’re excited to help users express themselves and gain access to these tools. Googlebooks come with pre-installed tooling to get you going. In this post, we’ll explore the capabilities of our new Linux terminal— now available in preview— share our future roadmap, and invite you to help us shape this ecosystem together.

Entry point for agentic development

AI agents use the terminal to install packages, write files, automate tasks, and create apps based on prompts written in plain language. For Googlebook to be the perfect companion for building and working at the frontier of agentic AI, the terminal needed to be easily accessible.

We understand AI comes with risks. Googlebook OS has been architected with defense-in-depth as a core principle. All terminal commands run entirely inside the Linux VM, creating an isolated sandbox. This design allows users to grant `sudo` (administrator) privileges to AI tools like Antigravity and other agentic AI platforms, that make heavy use of command-line tools, while limiting opportunities for system corruption or unauthorized access to your private files. The VM boundary helps protect the host OS and unmounted files; each directory made available to the Linux VM is only mounted after the user’s explicit permission. Best of all, a one-click VM reset makes experimentation stress free because users can easily retain their files on the host file system when they reset the VM. You can even see your Linux files inside the Googlebook Files app, where a user can access local folders – including photos and files synced effortlessly from their Android phone. Using a quick Python script or AI agent, you can batch-process your files in seconds.

Linux VM benefits

The terminal provides users with the freedom to create and use the software that they choose. We’re excited to see users build tools that are hyper-specific to their needs as well as prototype apps for broader use. With a Debian Linux environment, users benefit from the mature ecosystem familiar to Linux developers. This means that they have access to the latest CLI tools and common developer workflows like `apt`, `git`, `ssh`, and common compilers and runtimes.

Out of the box, our preview of the terminal on Googlebook has been optimized for rapid prototyping, web development, scripting, and agentic workflows via CLI. There is automatic localhost port forwarding to the host browser, and support for modern runtimes (e.g., Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, Rust). Users can adjust the amount of memory made available to the VM to best suit their workloads. Our own engineers have been using Googlebooks to build a Linux kernel and use the terminal for platform engineering.

Looking ahead

We can’t wait for the terminal and Linux VM to continue getting more capable over time, including Linux GUI app support with integration directly into the app launcher. Here are some key areas on the roadmap:

We are working hard to get you building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices. In addition to the existing network passthrough and wireless ADB, USB passthrough and support for ADB over USB are coming, enabling local device debugging and more from our Linux VM and Antigravity. Learn more about Antigravity on Googlebook.

Our testers have been eager to run more complex tasks. To make this more seamless, we are adding dynamic memory and storage scaling for the VM.

We will be adding GPU/NPU hardware acceleration for heavier local workloads, allowing users to leverage the performance and power efficiency of dedicated hardware.

VM persistence and separation from the terminal window will better support long-running processes, when you want to take on more demanding agentic workloads.

We’re looking forward to seeing your creations and will be sharing more soon. Questions? You can reach us here for direct support. We've also really enjoyed hearing your early thoughts and feedback in r/googlebook.

items.title: Introducing TimesFM 3.0 with multivariate time-series forecasting in BigQuery
items.text:
Overview

Since introducing zero-shot time-series forecasting in BigQuery with AI.FORECAST — initially powered by TimesFM 2.0 and later upgraded to TimesFM 2.5 — you have been able to generate forecasts directly in SQL without training or managing custom models. However, up until TimesFM 2.5, these foundation models were limited to univariate forecasting, predicting future values from the history of a single time series alone. In practice, most real-world forecasting problems are multivariate, where related targets and external drivers like weather, promotions, and holidays jointly shape future outcomes.

Today, we are thrilled to announce the preview of TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery. Developed by Google Research, TimesFM 3.0 is a 330-million parameter state-of-the-art foundation model designed to unlock native multivariate time-series forecasting directly inside BigQuery SQL. TimesFM 3.0 ranks #1 across all three major public time-series leaderboards — GIFT-Eval, FEV-Bench, and TIME — achieving top zero-shot accuracy on both covariate and multivariate forecasting tasks compared to existing foundation models.

Alongside its new multivariate capabilities, TimesFM 3.0 also serves as a drop-in upgrade for univariate forecasting via AI.FORECAST and anomaly detection via AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES. Existing workflows can immediately benefit from higher benchmark accuracy simply by specifying model => 'TimesFM 3.0'.

What’s new: Multivariate foundation modeling

With TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings enterprise-grade multivariate modeling into familiar SQL workflows via AI.FORECAST:

Capability

TimesFM 2.0 / 2.5

TimesFM 3.0

Forecasting scope

Univariate only

Univariate and multivariate

Target columns

Single target

Single or multiple targets

Covariate columns with past-only values

Not supported

Supported

Covariate columns with past and future values

Not supported

Supported

Multivariate forecasting with BigQuery SQL

To see how these capabilities work together, let’s forecast daily commuter (subscriber_trips) and leisure (casual_trips) bike rides over a seven-day horizon using the NYC Citi Bike public dataset (bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips).

BigQuery uses a single-table input format for multivariate forecasting that combines two sets of rows:

Historical observation rows: timestamps between start time (2016-01-01) and the forecast cutoff date (2016-06-01), fully populated with target metrics, past covariates, and known future covariates

Future horizon rows: timestamps across the seven-day forecast horizon (2016-06-01 to 2016-06-07) populated with known future covariates, while target columns and past-only covariates are set to NULL

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "WITH data AS (\r\n SELECT\r\n DATE(starttime) AS date,\r\n IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Subscriber'), NULL) AS subscriber_trips,\r\n IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Customer'), NULL) AS casual_trips,\r\n IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', AVG(tripduration / 60.0), NULL) AS avg_duration_min,\r\n IF(EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM MIN(starttime)) IN (1, 7), 1.0, 0.0) AS is_weekend\r\n FROM `bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips`\r\n WHERE starttime >= '2016-01-01' AND starttime < '2016-06-08'\r\n GROUP BY date\r\n)\r\nSELECT\r\n *\r\nFROM\r\n AI.FORECAST(\r\n TABLE data,\r\n MODEL => 'TimesFM 3.0',\r\n TIMESTAMP_COL => 'date',\r\n TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'],\r\n PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'],\r\n FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend']\r\n );"), ('language', 'lang-sql'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f60fe30aed0>)])]>

This query highlights the three multivariate dimensions supported in TimesFM 3.0:

Forecasting correlated targets (target_cols) Instead of running separate models for each rider segment, passing TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'] forecasts both metrics jointly in a single call. TimesFM 3.0 captures the cross-series dynamics between commuter and casual riders — such as shared weather sensitivity and diverging weekend ridership patterns.

Using past covariates (past_covariate_cols) Some signals can only be observed historically and are not known in advance, such as average ride duration (avg_duration_min), historical foot traffic, or unplanned service disruptions. Passing PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'] (with future horizon rows set to NULL) gives the model historical context to distinguish temporary shocks from underlying trends without requiring future values for that feature.

Using future covariates (future_covariate_cols) Other external drivers are known ahead of time across both the historical window and the forecast horizon — such as weekends (is_weekend), holidays, or scheduled promotions. Passing FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend'] (populated across all rows through 2016-06-07) allows TimesFM 3.0 to condition its seven-day predictions directly on upcoming calendar events.

Understanding the output

The function returns structured predictions for each target column specified in target_cols. For each column in target_cols, AI.FORECAST returns a struct containing the point forecast (value) and the lower and upper prediction interval bounds:

subscriber_

trips.value

subscriber_trips.prediction_

subscriber_trips.prediction_

interval_upper_bound

casual_trips.value

casual_trips.prediction_

interval_lower_bound

casual_trips.prediction_

interval_upper_bound

time_series_type

confidence_level
