TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics

You can also run multivariate forecasts using natural language in BigQuery Conversational Analytics. On the same bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips dataset, you can simply ask "Forecast both daily subscriber and casual trips for June 1–7, 2016 using two month historical data, with average trip duration as a past covariate and weekend indicator as a future covariate." Conversational Analytics automatically generates and executes the underlying AI.FORECAST query with TimesFM 3.0, returning a summary of the results, interactive forecast charts with prediction intervals for each target, and key forecast insights.

Multivariate forecasting with TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics, generating 7-day predictions, interactive charts, and insights from a natural-language prompt.

Summary and next steps

With native multivariate support in TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings state-of-the-art foundation model forecasting to complex, interconnected enterprise datasets without requiring data movement, custom feature engineering pipelines, or dedicated model hosting infrastructure.

To start forecasting with TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery:

Read the Google Research blog post to learn more about the TimesFM 3.0 model architecture and capabilities.

Explore the BigQuery TimesFM documentation.

Follow the step-by-step multivariate forecasting tutorial.

Try AI.FORECAST with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` directly in the BigQuery Studio SQL workspace.

Try AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` for univariate time series anomaly detection in BigQuery.

Try AI.EVALUATE with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` for univariate time series evaluation in BigQuery.

items.title: Trusted Data Apps for the Agentic Data Cloud, powered by Looker
items.text:
As a business intelligence user, this probably sounds familiar: Most dashboards only provide you with a standardized canvas and a fixed library of charts, and the “analysis” consists of a CSV export that takes you to another system. Or sometimes it's designing the dashboard that’s the challenge: You can picture the executive briefing, the customer-facing portal, or the interactive explainer that you want, but can’t assemble it out of the available grid tiles.

Either way, the solution has always been to build a custom application. The advent of AI has sped up the process — a working prototype now takes an afternoon — but the excitement of that first demo fades fast. Without access to governed data, row-level security, an infrastructure owner, or a clear path through security review, a tool written by an LLM is simply a prototype that can never go to production.

Today, to bridge this gap, we are announcing Looker Data Apps (in preview) — pairing the speed of agent-generated applications with the governance, security, and trust of your existing Looker governance framework. Describe what you need in plain language, and the agent builds it as a real, production-grade application hosted natively inside Looker!

What is a data app?

A data app is a bespoke, interactive web application generated by an AI agent and hosted natively within Looker. While dashboards provide top-down visibility, data apps serve as an active system of action designed around a specific operational workflow. A data app:

Goes beyond standard grid tiles with pixel-perfect, bespoke layouts configured for a specific operational role or job-to-be-done.

Enables business users to input parameters, test scenarios, run live simulations, and update underlying records.

Connects end-to-end business processes by connecting data analysis to business execution tasks like updating source records or dispatching events to tools like Salesforce and Jira.

Build pixel-perfect interfaces using AI developer tools like Claude Code or Antigravity CLI, grounded directly by Looker’s semantic layer.

Expanding your semantic layer into an application platform

Data apps do not replace dashboards; they expand the boundaries of what you can build on top of your existing dashboards and semantic layer.

Dashboards excel at aggregate visibility and passive reporting. Data apps handle active execution, letting users modify parameters and trigger downstream business tasks.

Dashboards provide consistency using standardized chart libraries. Data apps deliver broad flexibility, unlocking custom web components and specialized interactions.

Data apps are grounded in governed data to ensure accuracy. Whether users are reviewing a KPI dashboard or adjusting budgets in a data app, all logic is governed centrally with the LookML semantic layer to eliminate metric discrepancies and hallucinations.

Transform analysis into action with customizable, multi-page web app experiences and embedded operational workflows.

Built for enterprise scale

We designed Looker Data Apps for demanding, governed enterprises.

Every measure is grounded in the semantic layer. Every app you build directly inherits your existing semantic models, row-level security, and access controls. Calculations stay consistent across the enterprise, and built-in query inspection lets teams audit every line of generated SQL to eliminate metric hallucinations.

Zero-code by default. Deploy agent-generated React applications directly inside Looker with no code. Or users can use LLMs like Claude Code and Antigravity CLI to build interactive apps and deploy them as data apps in minutes.

No runtime token costs. LLM tokens are only consumed when you’re designing or generating the app. After that, every end-user interaction runs on native Looker APIs and models. Put a data app in front of 50 people or 5,000 and the marginal cost doesn't change.

As easy as embedding a dashboard. You can deploy your data apps into external portals using the same workflows you use to embed a dashboard. No new pipelines, no custom application code, no second permission models.

From prototype to production in minutes

The days of having to choose between basic dashboards and investing valuable engineering time to build bespoke systems are coming to an end. Instead of letting prototypes stall in sandboxes due to compliance and security barriers, Looker Data Apps allows teams to deploy governed, production-grade tools in minutes.

Looker Data Apps are now in preview. Get started today.

items.title: 10 Years of the SRE book: Announcing the second edition of "Site Reliability Engineering”
items.text:
A decade ago, Google released Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems with O'Reilly Media. What began as a collection of our practices for managing large-scale infrastructure became a bestselling book, and inspired many organizations to adopt the reliability practices it outlined: applying software engineering to operations to build systems that are scalable, reliable, and sustainable.

Over the past ten years, computing landscapes have undergone profound shifts. AI, microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless paradigms, and platform engineering have all reshaped how we build and operate software. To mark the 10th anniversary of the book's release, we are excited to announce the completely rewritten second edition of the Google SRE book, reflecting a decade of lessons learned both inside Google and across the broader industry, to offer fresh guidance tailored for today's operational challenges.

Why update the book?

When we published the first edition, many organizations were focused on early cloud migrations and just starting to transition from monolithic architectures. Today, with organizations delivering software at a high velocity and at global scale, the challenge is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining high reliability in the face of the immense complexity.

Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before. The explosion of resource-intensive workloads like generative AI has changed the economics and operational requirements of infrastructure management.

Writing this second edition required us to take a step back and evaluate what it takes to successfully implement SRE today.

A decade of evolution: How SRE practices have progressed

The second edition takes a deep dive into how foundational site reliability engineering practices have matured over the last ten years, shifting from manual, task-specific work toward automated, platform-wide capabilities. Consider, for example:

SLOs and error budgets: In 2016, teams relied on basic availability metrics and manual error budget policies. Today, practices have matured into user-centric, multi-tiered SLOs with dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement.

Monitoring and observability: Early setups centered on static dashboards, basic logs, and manual alert triage. Modern observability leverages OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing, and automated anomaly correlation to find root causes quickly.

Automation and platforms: Operations have shifted from writing custom scripts for isolated tasks to using declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms, and resilient, self-healing systems.

Reliability testing: Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification.

Capacity and resource management: Manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment, and dedicated cost and cluster optimization for GPU and TPU workloads.

Organizational models: SRE has expanded beyond dedicated teams assigned to specific applications. Today's organizations use hybrid models, platform engineering integrations, and reliability champions embedded across product teams.

SRE in the age of AI

Then there’s the dual relationship between SRE and artificial Intelligence: how SRE supports AI infrastructure, and how SRE teams use AI to enhance operational reliability.

Running large language models (LLMs) and foundation models introduces novel reliability challenges. The book outlines methodologies for operating AI infrastructure at scale:

Managing massive GPU and TPU hardware cluster reliability and network topologies

Monitoring non-deterministic outputs and latency characteristics unique to AI

Ensuring pipeline reliability for continuous model training, fine-tuning, and data processing

AI is also rapidly becoming a force multiplier for reliability engineers. The second edition shares practical frameworks for enhancing human operational efficiency:

Using generative AI tools to assist in real-time incident triage and postmortem generation

Interrogating complex system telemetry using natural language queries

Using predictive machine learning models to identify resource bottlenecks before outages occur

What hasn’t changed? The importance of culture

While technologies and architectures continuously evolve, the core principles of SRE remain intact, and are key to establishing a reliability-focused culture. Accordingly, the second edition re-emphasizes and expands upon the human elements of system engineering, and how to get there.

Whether you’re new to the field, a practitioner, an engineering manager, or a technology executive, the rewritten second edition of Site Reliability Engineering serves as your definitive roadmap for the next era of production systems.

You can order your copy today in physical format (see Google Books) or digital format from O'Reilly.

items.title: Agentic data science with the Data Agent Kit
items.text:
Imagine your compliance team notices that payments are taking longer than expected to clear. They suspect fraud, and you’re the data scientist helping figure out which transactions to investigate first. Assembling that shortlist requires ingesting and cleaning raw transaction logs, training a model on past fraud, scoring new records, and scheduling the pipeline to run daily. Here’s how you can build that workflow end to end with an agent, using the Data Agent Kit inside the Antigravity IDE.

Introducing the Data Agent Kit

Data Agent Kit helps you work with Google Cloud data through a plugin for coding agents or an extension for Visual Studio Code-based IDEs. It brings two significant additions to the workflow:

Help for your agent: MCP tools connect your agent to data services. Skills are Markdown files that give it instructions and best practices for working with your data stack

Tools in your IDE: work with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud, from querying databases to deploying an Airflow pipeline, without leaving your editor

Loading the data

Let’s start with the raw transaction logs in Google Cloud Storage. You can ask the agent to create a notebook that loads them into BigQuery using Spark:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to ingest JSON transaction logs from gs://financials-clearing-raw/ into the BigQuery table transactions.raw_transactions.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f60fe32fd50>)])]>

The agent generates a Jupyter notebook that loads the JSON logs into a BigQuery table named raw_transactions. You can open the notebook, review the code, and run it using a preconfigured Spark Serverless runtime from the IDE.

Running a generated PySpark notebook

After the notebook runs, you can open the raw_transactions table with the Data Agent Kit. The extension allows you to browse the table and inspect its metadata right from the IDE.

Inspecting a BigQuery table in the IDE

The records are now in BigQuery, but they aren’t ready for model training yet. First, we’ll handle duplicate and incomplete records, then join the remaining records with info about who sent and received each payment.

Cleaning it up

Let’s put the cleanup logic into a dbt project so we can run it on each new batch of data. We’ll also test that each transaction appears only once. Prompt the agent:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a dbt project in dbt_project/ for the BigQuery dataset transactions.\r\n\r\nDeduplicate raw_transactions by transaction_id in staging. Separate records with null IDs into invalid_transactions. Join valid records with dim_payers and dim_payees to create enriched_transactions, preserving the is_fraud label. Add a transaction uniqueness test.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f60fe32c5d0>)])]>

The agent generates a dbt project with SQL models for cleaning and enriching the data. Take a look at the generated code to check how it handles duplicates and joins reference tables. Then run dbt build in the terminal. This builds the staging and enriched tables in BigQuery, along with a separate table for records with missing transaction IDs. dbt also runs the uniqueness test.

Validating dbt models in the integrated terminal

We also keep the is_fraud column, which indicates whether a past transaction was fraudulent. We’ll train the model on records with known labels and use it to score new transactions, where we’re unsure yet whether fraud occurred.

Building the review queue

With the data prepared, let’s ask the agent to create a training notebook using a Random Forest classifier running on Spark Serverless.

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to train a RandomForestClassifier\r\non table transactions.enriched_transactions.\r\n\r\nPredict is_fraud, training only on records where the label\r\nis not null. Encode categorical features, scale amounts,\r\nand evaluate the model using ROC AUC. Save the evaluated model to gs://models/fraud_model.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f60fe32e450>)])]>

Review and run the notebook, then check its evaluation output to see how well the model separates fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones. You can also use the Data Agent Kit extension to verify that the trained model artifacts were saved to Google Cloud Storage.

Verifying the trained model artifacts in Google Cloud Storage

Now we can use the saved model to score transactions that don’t have an is_fraud value yet:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a batch inference notebook that loads the saved model from gs://my_models/fraud_model and scores records in transactions.enriched_transactions where is_fraud is null.\r\n\r\nWrite transactions with a fraud probability score >= 0.50 to the Spanner table SparkEvalFraudReviewQueue, in the instance cymbal-fraud, database fraud-db.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f60fe32f1d0>)])]>

In this example, the inference notebook scores the unlabeled transactions in BigQuery and sends those with an estimated fraud probability of 50% or higher to the Spanner review queue. The flagged records help the team decide where to investigate, but they still need to determine whether fraud occurred.

Look at how the inference notebook filters and writes flagged records, then run it. Once it finishes, query the Spanner table in the IDE to inspect the results.

Querying flagged transactions in the Spanner table

This table is the list we set out to build. The compliance team can now start reviewing transactions, and we have a workflow that gets records from raw logs into the queue.

So far, we have been kicking off each step ourselves. We can now connect them so the workflow runs automatically each day.

Running it again tomorrow

Each day we will load the latest logs, apply the dbt transformations, and score unlabeled transactions using the saved model. We’ll use the Managed Service for Apache Airflow to run these steps in order. Ask the agent:

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create an orchestration pipeline named fraud_analysis_pipeline that runs ingestion, the dbt project, and batch inference in that order.\r\n\r\nSchedule it daily at midnight. Use Spark Serverless for the notebooks, including the Spanner connector for inference, and gs://YOUR_ARTIFACT_BUCKET for artifact storage.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f60fe32c650>)])]>

The agent generates a YAML pipeline definition and deployment configuration. The pipeline definition sets the schedule and dependencies between steps. Meanwhile, the deployment configuration specifies the Airflow environment where it will run.

Data Agent Kit then turns the definition into an Airflow DAG, which you can explore as an interactive graph in the IDE. Open the pipeline under “Orchestration Pipelines” and click a task to inspect it. For notebook tasks, you can follow the link straight back to the code.

Inspecting a data pipeline

With the Airflow environment configured, click “Run pipeline” in the canvas. Data Agent Kit packages the notebooks and dbt project, deploys the DAG, and triggers a run. Open the pipeline’s execution history to follow its progress. You can also select individual tasks to inspect their status, duration, and logs.

Kicking off an Airflow DAG and inspecting the logs

Airflow will run the pipeline every day, taking new batches of data from raw logs to the review queue. The compliance team can now focus on flagged transactions, and you’ve automated the work of getting those records to them!

Try it yourself

If you are ready to try this for yourself, we have designed a codelab that walks you through the full setup so you can build and run this workflow. You can also read our documentation or check out the skills and tools in the open-source repository on GitHub.

items.title: Google Meet now uses post-quantum cryptography
items.text:
Calls in Google Meet will use post-quantum cryptography (PQC) for extra protection, starting now with laptop web clients and meeting room hardware, with mobile support coming soon. There are no visible changes, and you can continue using Meet normally. The updated encryption protects your data against potential future quantum computer threats.

The expansion of PQC to all Meet calls will help to secure infrastructure and services against the potential threat of a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer. No such computer exists today; however this change helps protect today's Meet traffic from the theoretical risk of being harvested and decrypted by a future quantum computer, an approach commonly referred to as Store Now, Decrypt Later.

Google Meet has used quantum-safe encryption previously for client-side encrypted calls (CSE).

Google automatically implements all necessary updates to benefit all Meet hosts and participants. Administrators and end users don't need to take any action.

Getting started

Admins: There is no admin control for this feature.

End users: There is no end user setting for this feature. Visit the Help Center to learn more about call & meeting encryption in Google Meet.

Rollout pace

Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains: Gradual rollout (up to 15 days for feature visibility) starting on Oct 12 for web and room hardware

Availability

Available to all Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and users with personal Google accounts

Announcement

OAuth 2.0 clients calling the Google Docs Model Context Protocol (MCP) server are required to have Use this client for an AI-powered agent selected in Google Auth Platform > Clients.

Starting November 11, 2026, Google Workspace MCP servers will reject requests from any app or integration whose OAuth client is not marked as agentic by selecting Use this client for an AI-powered agent. OAuth clients that are not marked as agentic by November 12, 2026 will remain non-agentic and can't call Google Workspace MCP servers. To use MCP after this date, you will need to create a new OAuth client marked as agentic and update your app to use it.

Apps and integrations that are not AI agents, like those that only call Google Workspace REST APIs, are not affected by this change. If an existing OAuth client is used for both AI agent and non-agent features, create a separate OAuth client for the AI agent and mark only that client as agentic. Keep the existing client for your non-agent features.

The Google Docs MCP server is available as part of the Developer Preview Program. For instructions on configuring an OAuth 2.0 client for the Google Docs MCP server, see Set up the Google Docs MCP server and Manage OAuth Clients.

items.title: Google Workspace Weekly Recap - October 9, 2026
items.text:
Secondary calendars will now follow the lifecycle of their owner

As announced earlier this year, we are now rolling out the secondary calendar lifecycle changes for non-personal Workspace accounts: secondary calendars will now follow the lifecycle of their owner, meaning that when a user account is deleted, any secondary calendars owned by that user will be deleted as well. | Learn more.

Preview, edit and collaborate on Markdown (.md) files natively across Drive and Docs

We are introducing the ability to view, edit, and collaborate on Markdown (.md or .markdown) files directly in Google Docs, as well as view rendered previews in Google Drive. | Learn more.

Use stock charts in Sheets to better visualize price movements

Google Sheets now supports new types of stock charts, making it easier to visualize price movement over time. Stock charts condense several price points for each time period into a single marker, so you can read a security's full trading range at a glance rather than interpreting separate line series. | Learn more.

Create Trello cards from Google Chat messages with Trello for Google Workspace

Trello for Google Workspace makes it easy to capture tasks and ideas from the conversations where they begin. With the app, you can create new Trello cards from emails and Google Chat messages, helping you keep Trello up to date without switching tabs or breaking your flow. | Learn more.

Point-in-time editing now available in Google Vids

Google Vids is improving the video creation experience with the introduction of point-in-time editing. This feature will help ensure that the canvas matches the video timeline 1:1. Previously, the canvas displayed all elements present across an entire scene all at the same time, regardless of when they appeared during the video. | Learn more.

Carrier Link for Google Voice available in 14 additional countries

In June, we launched Carrier Link in 20 countries where Google Voice service was not otherwise available. Today, we are making Carrier Link available in an additional 14 countries (the US, Canada, and much of Europe). Previously, customers in these countries could purchase Google Voice with a first party calling plan provided by Google. Now, customers who want the simplicity and features of Google Voice, but would prefer to use it in combination with a calling plan purchased from a local carrier can do so. | Learn more.

New logic and search steps in Workspace Studio help expand automation capabilities

We are introducing several new feature enhancements to Google Workspace Studio as part of the October 2026 feature release. These additions expand automation capabilities across Gmail, Google Meet, Google Drive, and custom control logic, giving users more flexibility to build sophisticated workflows without writing code. | Learn more.

The announcements above were published on the Workspace Updates blog over the last week. Please refer to the original blog posts for complete details.

items.title: New logic and search steps in Workspace Studio help expand automation capabilities
items.text:
We are introducing several new feature enhancements to Google Workspace Studio as part of the October 2026 feature release. These additions expand automation capabilities across Gmail, Google Meet, Google Drive, and custom control logic, giving users more flexibility to build sophisticated workflows without writing code.

Specifically, this release includes:

Nested Conditionals: Enables nested branching logic within flows so users can build multi-layered conditional decision paths.

Gmail Skip Replies: Allows users to configure Gmail thread triggers to ignore follow-up replies, ensuring flows trigger only on primary incoming emails.

Meet Calendar Outputs: Expands the Google Meet primitive to output additional Calendar event metadata—including full invitee lists—and provides template support for generating post-meeting follow-up email drafts.

Search for a Doc: Introduces a dedicated Google Drive step that allows flows to search dynamically for relevant document files based on search parameters.

These enhancements eliminate repetitive follow-up tasks, allow dynamic document lookup, and provide more control over automated communication across Google Workspace.

Getting started

Admins: Feature controls inherit overall Workspace Studio domain and OU-level policies. Admin settings for prerequisite primitives ramped prior to feature deployment. Visit the Help Center to learn more.

End users: Features are ON by default and accessible directly within the Workspace Studio flow builder. Visit the Help Center to learn more.

Rollout pace

Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains: Gradual rollout (up to 15 days for feature visibility) starting on October 13, 2026

Availability

Available to all Google Workspace customers and Workspace Individual subscribers with access to Google Workspace Studio.

items.title: Modernizing Unstructured Data Workflows: Alteryx Live Query meets Google Cloud BigQuery
items.text:
Alteryx One Live Query and Google Cloud BigQuery redefine how enterprises handle complex, unstructured data at scale by reducing reliance on disconnected tools, minimizing data movement, and enabling warehouse-native execution.

Live Query provides an intuitive, browser-based environment that allows business users to build sophisticated data pipelines without writing a single line of code. When paired with the scale and performance of BigQuery, this duo enables secure SQL pushdown, meaning data transformation logic is executed directly within the warehouse rather than moving it across the network. This synergy is particularly potent for document-heavy workflows, where Live Query can orchestrate Google’s advanced AI and machine learning models — like Gemini — to extract intelligence from PDFs and images while maintaining the strict data governance and security of the BigQuery environment.

From invoice PDFs to govern exception reporting in BigQuery with Live Query

Finance and operations teams often find themselves buried under a mountain of vendor invoices. These documents come as PDFs with inconsistent data, varying invoice number formats, and a high risk of manual error. Traditionally, data teams have had to resort to manual data extraction or use a fragmented series of tools to move data into a warehouse — a process that is both time-consuming and prone to duplicates or amount mismatches.

With the integration of Live Query for BigQuery, you can now automate the entire lifecycle of an invoice. By processing PDFs, extracting key fields, and standardizing results directly within the BigQuery ecosystem, data teams can identify exceptions like anomalies or data issues within the documents faster while ensuring their governed enterprise data configured through the BigQuery fine grained access policies never has to leave the warehouse.

Solution overview: Extract, classify, validate, route, and post

Let’s dive deeper into how the Live Query solution works. Invoice PDFs arrive as unstructured documents in Google Cloud Storage. In the Live Query workflow, the Document Extract tool extracts structured fields using the model selected by the user, such as Gemini or Document AI. The results are then standardized for reliable matching and compared against historical invoice records already stored and governed in BigQuery.

This automated workflow is designed to move from document to decision with minimal manual intervention. At enterprise scale, that pattern is not just about processing a handful of PDFs — it is about enabling analytics and AI over millions of unstructured documents while keeping reconciliation logic aligned with BigQuery.

By combining AI-driven extraction with BigQuery-native execution, the solution provides:

Higher straight-through processing: Reducing manual handling and allowing more invoices to move through the process automatically.

Faster reconciliation and fewer manual exceptions: Comparing extracted invoices against BigQuery data earlier in the process so teams can identify duplicates and mismatches sooner, reducing the number of invoices that require manual review.

Stronger auditability: Maintaining a clear trail of data from source to operational output.

Reduced data movement: Keeping data resident in BigQuery and leverage its built-in capabilities for enhanced security, governance, and control.

Architecture: A Google Cloud-native pattern

At a high level, invoice PDFs are staged in Cloud Storage, processed through a Live Query workflow in the browser, reconciled against governed invoice history already resident in BigQuery, and written back as operational outputs for finance teams. The key architectural advantage of this pattern is that workflow authoring happens in the browser, while transformation and reconciliation logic are executed through platform services against the governed data environment.

The Live Query architecture is designed for warehouse-scale processing and governed execution. It uses secure SQL pushdown to execute transformation and reconciliation logic directly in BigQuery, and integrates with Gemini for advanced AI capabilities such as document extraction, classification, and summarization.

Live Query (Browser): Users author workflows visually in the browser, configuring document extraction, classification, cleansing, validation, and routing logic.

Alteryx One Platform Services: The Transformation Service coordinates request handling, execution planning, and result retrieval between the browser workflow and the customer data environment. The services also add traceability and observability across workflow execution, strengthening both operational monitoring and auditability.

Customer Google Cloud: Invoice PDFs are staged in Google Cloud Storage (GCS), historical invoice data remains governed in BigQuery, AI-backed extraction runs against that environment, and the workflow outputs are written back into BigQuery.

In this pattern, the browser is the authoring layer, Alteryx One Platform Services are the coordination layer, and Google Cloud is the governed data and execution layer. It allows workflow logic to be authored visually in Live Query while execution remains aligned with governed data and warehouse-scale processing in BigQuery.

Live query workflow walkthrough: From PDF to insight

Let’s take a closer look at how the Live Query workflow handles unstructured PDFs, using an invoice as the example.

Ingest invoice PDFs

The workflow begins by pointing to a directory input in Google Cloud Storage, where the raw PDF files are stored. In practice, this step does more than just identify a folder: it enumerates the PDF locations and returns file-level metadata — such as absolute file paths, size, and created / updated timestamps — so the workflow can reliably pass the right document set into downstream extraction steps.

Extract key fields

Using Alteryx’s Document Extract tool, the workflow processes PDF invoices stored in Google Cloud Storage and extracts structured or semi-structured results directly in BigQuery. The extraction step uses the user-selected model, either Document AI or Gemini AI, depending on the workflow configuration. Under the hood, the tool builds a temporary external object table from the input document URIs and executes the appropriate function — ML.PROCESS_DOCUMENT for Document AI model or AI.GENERATE for Gemini AI model. For this workflow, the Gemini path is used, with AI.GENERATE returning the requested invoice fields into the downstream Live Query workflow.

During interactive design, Live Query limits processing to a small subset of document URIs for preview, while runtime execution processes the full set of invoice PDFs.

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- illustrative pattern only\r\nSELECT *\r\nFROM AI.GENERATE(\r\n MODEL project.dataset.gemini_model,\r\n (\r\n SELECT\r\n uri,\r\n 'Extract invoice_number, invoice_amount, vendor_name, net_amount, tax_amount, and line_items.' AS prompt\r\n FROM project.dataset.temp_invoice_object_table\r\n )\r\n);"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f404b475cd0>)])]>

Classify extracted content

After extraction, the workflow uses Alteryx’s Classify tool to apply zero-shot classification to the extracted invoice text. In this use case, line-item content is labeled into predefined business categories — such as industrial or office supplies — using AI.CLASSIFY in BigQuery, which returns a new predicted-label column into the downstream workflow. This business context makes the extracted data more useful for downstream reconciliation, exception handling, and reporting.

code_block

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- illustrative pattern only\r\nSELECT *,\r\n AI.CLASSIFY(line_item_text, categories => ['industrial', 'office']) AS line_item_classify\r\nFROM upstream"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f404a94bf90>)])]>

Normalize data

The extracted invoice numbers are cleansed and standardized so that minor formatting differences — such as whitespace or inconsistent formatting — do not hide potential duplicates during reconciliation.

Compare against history

The workflow joins the normalized current invoice records against historical invoice data already resident in BigQuery. This reconciliation step identifies records with matching invoice numbers already present in history and flags them as potential duplicates.

Flag exceptions

A formula step then applies business-rule logic to the remaining records. Those rules can vary by workflow and may include checks for amount mismatches, missing required fields, invalid totals, or other finance-specific exceptions. In this example, one rule checks whether invoice_amount matches net_amount + tax_amount and flags mismatches for review.

Produce operational outputs

The workflow produces two operational outputs: one for invoices matched to historical records and flagged as potential duplicates, and another for unmatched current invoices that have been validated, labeled for exceptions where needed, and prepared for unpaid-invoice processing.

The result is not just extracted data, but governed operational outputs that finance teams can review and act on immediately.

Summary: A governed document-to-decision workflow

Our joint customers are excited for these new capabilities that will help improve business processes.

“What stood out to me about Alteryx One: Google Edition was how naturally it fits into the Google Cloud experience. I'm excited about the opportunity to make analytics more accessible by enabling business users to work with BigQuery data through an intuitive, governed experience.” - Michael Wyant, Vice President, Enterprise Data & Corporate Solutions, Papa Johns

This use case is more than just a simple extraction tool; it represents a strong Google Cloud-native pattern for transforming unstructured documents into actionable operational outputs. Instead of moving warehouse data into disconnected preparation tools, the workflow keeps storage, extraction, reconciliation, and output generation aligned with governed enterprise data already resident in BigQuery. By combining the intuitive design of Alteryx One Live Query with the scale and AI capabilities of BigQuery, finance teams can reduce manual effort, accelerate exception handling, and focus on higher-value strategic initiatives.

items.text:
In June, we launched Carrier Link in 20 countries where Google Voice service was not otherwise available. Today, we are making Carrier Link available in an additional 14 countries (the US, Canada, and much of Europe). Previously, customers in these countries could purchase Google Voice with a first party calling plan provided by Google. Now, customers who want the simplicity and features of Google Voice, but would prefer to use it in combination with a calling plan purchased from a local carrier can do so.

Our partners Southlight Services, Gamma Communications, Tata Communications & Telefonica Global Solutions have collaborated with Google Voice to offer these services in these countries.

Carrier Link allows Workspace customers to easily add phone numbers and calling plans from a certified local carrier, leveraging a pre-configured multi-tenant implementation of SIP Link.

This simplifies the process of setting up a cloud phone system, allowing customers to make and receive calls with payment handled by their local carrier and minimal configuration. Carrier Link is especially helpful for small businesses that want a reliable connection without the hassle of setting up their own hardware.

Getting started

Admins: Contact one of our Carrier Link partners to get started. They will provision the SIP Link licenses and phone numbers, which you can then assign to users, desk phones, auto-attendants, and ring groups. Visit the Help Center to learn more about Carrier Link requirements.

End users: There is no end user action required.

Rollout pace
